items.title: Colorado wildlife overpass cut vehicle-animal collisions by 91%, report finds
items.summary: Elk, bear, frogs and other animals have used the overpass, which connects 39,000 acres of habitat, since its completion Colorado officials have tracked herds of elk, bears, pronghorn and even northern leopard frogs ambling across its new wildlife overpass. According to a newly released report, the overpass, which acts as a bridge over a busy stretch of interstate, has helped cut wildlife-vehicle collisions by 91% since its completion 10 months ago. The overpass is the centerpiece of a larger system built by the state to assist wildlife crossing the highway, which also includes miles of 8-ft tall fencing and five large wildlife underpasses. Continue reading...

items.summary: 대전 유성구 화암동 호남고속도로 북대전IC 인근에서 2.5t 화물차가 도로 작업 중이던 사다리차를 들이받는 사고가 발생했다. 경찰 등에 따르면 19일 오후 11시 2분경 이같은 사고가 났다. 이 사고로 현장에 있던 30대 신호수가 심정지 상태로 병원으로 이송됐으나 숨졌다. 화물차 운전자(50대)도 크게 다쳐 병원 치료를 받고 있다.경찰은 운전자가 급하게 차로를 변경한 앞차를 피하기 위해 방향을 틀다가 사고가 난 것으로 보고 정확한 사고 경위를 조사 중이다.

items.summary: 커피 프랜차이즈 할리스에서 과거 멤버십 개편용으로 만든 임시 데이터 파일이 유출됐다. 개인정보의 수집부터 보관, 파기까지 전 과정에 걸친 관리 소홀 문제가 또다시 수면 위로 올랐다.앞서 쿠팡 유출 사고에서도 탈퇴한 회원의 정보를 제때 파기하지 않고 남겨둔 사실이 드러난 바 있다. 해킹을 막는 기술 보안도 중요하지만 불필요한 개인정보를 제때 지우는 관리가 더 중요하다는 지적이 나온다.20일 할리스에 따르면 회사는 지난 16일 멤버십 정보를 사용하는 클라우드 서비스에서 인가되지 않은 접근이 발생해 개인정보가 유출된 사실을 확인했다.할리스가 한국인터넷진흥원(KISA)에 신고한 규모는 중복 회원을 포함해 약 276만건이다. 회사는 2009년부터 2020년 2월11일까지 누적된 고객 데이터로 추정하고 있다.할리스는 유출 자료가 현재 운영 중인 고객 데이터베이스(DB)가 아닌 과거 멤버십 서비스 개편을 위해 제공한 임시 데이터 파일인 것으로 파악하고 있다. 유출 항목에는 아이디와 비밀

items.title: “40년前 군대보다 건더기 적어”…휴게소 미역국에 분노
items.summary: 고속도로 휴게소에서 소고기 미역국을 주문한 소비자가 고기가 지나치게 적게 들어 있다며 불만을 제기했다.18일 한 온라인 커뮤니티에는 ‘어느 고속도로휴게소 소고기미역국’이라는 제목의 글이 올라왔다.글 작성자는 휴게소 이름을 공개하지 않은 채 “소고기 미역국을 시키고 건더기를 건져봤다”며 사진을 함께 올렸다. 사진에는 공깃밥 뚜껑 위에 미역국에서 건져낸 소고기가 몇 조각 놓여 있다.작성자는 “썩을 X들아, 40년 전 부대 취사병이 끓여준 것보다 고기가 없다”며 불만을 드러냈다. 이어 “정부에서 고속도로 휴게소 음식 손보겠다고 했는데 언제쯤 서민들이 체감할 수 있을까요?”라고 적었다.게시글을 접한 누리꾼들은 휴게소 음식의 양과 가격 등을 지적하며 불만을 나타냈다. 온라인에는 “고속도로 휴게소에서는 볼일만 봐야 한다”, “어느 순간부터 휴게소에서 안 사 먹게 된다”, “이러고 가격은 비싸게 받는다” 등의 반응을 보였다.

items.title: “요즘 누가 현장서 암표 파나요” 단속에도 ‘가을야구’ 암표 활개
items.summary: “요즘 누가 오프(오프라인)에서 암표를 파나요.”프로야구 포스트시즌(가을야구)이 지난 14일 본격 개막하면서 유관기관이 현장 암표 단속에 나섰다는 소식에 야구팬 최 모 씨(27·여)는 이같이 말했다.암표 거래가 단속에도 불구하고 사회관계망서비스(SNS)와 중고 거래 사이트 등을 온라인 등을 중심으로 활발히 이뤄지고 있다. 암표 거래를 통한 이득이 큰 이상 문제를 해소하기 쉽지 않을 것이란 지적이 나온다.‘마지막 잠실경기장’에 ‘가을야구’ 암표 횡행…SNS서 여전히 수십만원 거래20일 뉴스1 취재를 종합하면 유관기관 합동단속이 이뤄진 지난 14일 이후로도 온라인상에선 ‘가을야구’ 암표 거래가 활발하게 이어지고 있다.오는 12월 서울 잠실야구장이 돔 야구장 조성을 위한 철거에 들어가면서 마지막 잠실야구장 경기를 보려는 열기가 뜨거운 탓이다.이에 경찰, 문화체육관광부, 한국야구위원회(KBO) 등 유관기관은 잠실 더비 당일인 지난 14일 관계자 56명을 투입해 단속에 나섰으나

items.title: “학폭 가해자인줄”…흉기 소지하고 처음 본 행인 뒤따라간 40대 검거
items.summary: 일면식도 없는 행인을 해칠 목적으로 흉기 2점을 소지한 채 뒤따라간 40대 남성이 경찰에 붙잡혔다.대구 북부경찰서는 살인예비 혐의로 40대 남성을 검거해 조사하고 있다고 19일 밝혔다.이 남성은 지난 17일 오전 3시 30분경 대구 북구 산격동의 한 도로에서 흉기 2점을 소지한 채 처음 본 40대 남성을 약 10분간 뒤따라간 혐의를 받는다.뒤따라오는 남성의 행동을 수상하게 여긴 행인의 신고를 받고 출동한 경찰은 현장에서 불심검문을 실시해 흉기 2점을 소지한 사실을 확인하고 긴급체포했다.경찰 조사에서 이 남성은 과거 자신에게 학교폭력을 저지른 가해자를 해칠 목적으로 흉기를 들고 다니다 우연히 마주친 행인을 가해자로 착각해 뒤따라갔다는 취지로 진술한 것으로 알려졌다. 다만 그는 흉기를 꺼내 행인을 위협하거나 휘두르지는 않은 것으로 조사됐다.경찰은 정확한 범행 동기와 사건 경위를 조사하고 있다.

items.title: “이사비 150만원 냈는데 밥값도?”…포장이사 식사비 두고 엇갈린 반응
items.summary: 포장이사 업체에 이사 비용을 모두 지불했는데도 작업자들의 점심값을 챙겨달라는 부탁을 받았다는 사연이 전해져 누리꾼들의 반응이 엇갈리고 있다. 지난 18일 사회관계망서비스(SNS)에는 ‘이삿짐센터 직원들의 점심값을 내가 왜 줘야 하나’라는 취지의 글이 올라왔다.게시물을 작성한 A씨는 최근 포장이사를 맡겼다가 이사 당일 겪은 일을 공유했다. A씨에 따르면 이사 비용으로 150만원을 지불하고 작업자들에게 커피도 제공했지만, 점심시간이 되자 기사로부터 직원 4명의 밥값을 챙겨달라는 말을 들었다.A씨는 이사 비용을 이미 지불한 상황에서 작업자들의 식사 비용까지 따로 챙겨야 하는지 의문을 표했다. 정해진 서비스 비용 외에 식사 대접까지 고객이 신경 써야 하는 것이 당연한 일인지 이해하기 어렵다는 취지다.해당 사연을 접한 누리꾼들은 이사 업체로부터 음료나 간식 등을 요구받았던 경험을 공유하며 공감을 나타냈다.한 누리꾼은 “이삿짐센터 직원들이 계속 물 좀 사다 달라, 커피 좀 사다 달라

items.title: ‘마찰 없는 사회’ AI 시대… 몸이 던지는 불편한 질문
items.summary: 권병준 작가의 관객 참여형 전시 ‘자명리 공명 마을’에서 관객은 각자 헤드셋을 착용하고 전시 공간을 거닌다. 헤드셋에선 저마다 다른 음악이 흘러나온다. 다른 사람의 소리가 궁금하다면 가까이 다가가 인사를 건네면 된다. 그러면 두 사람의 소리가 교환된다. 기술을 활용한 전시지만, 정작 몸을 움직이지 않으면 아무 일도 일어나지 않는다. 관객을 연결하는 건 기술이 아니라 몸이다. 19일 서울 서초구 한국예술종합학교 서초캠퍼스. ‘자명리 공명 마을’의 사진이 화면에 뜨자 무용원 재학생 100여 명이 무용실기실에 모여 화면을 주목했다. 한예종 무용원이 개원 30주년을 맞아 16, 19, 20일 세 차례에 걸쳐 진행하는 강연 ‘몸, 그리고 내일’ 현장이다. 이날 강연에 나선 박지선 크리에이티브 프로듀서는 ‘기술시대에 몸을 어떻게 사유할 것인가’를 주제로 기술과 신체의 관계를 짚었다. 기술이 창작의 도구를 넘어 인간의 감각과 신체 경험까지 바꾸는 시대, 몸이 기반인 춤은 무엇을 지키고 무엇을

items.title: 산재 사망자 59%는 일용직… 안전모 안쓴채 1m 추락해 숨지기도

items.title: JB Pritzker thinks AI could help us live to 100 — or threaten us like nukes
items.summary: Today, I’m talking with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has a lot of thoughts about AI, tech, and privacy. If you’ve been listening to the show, you know that one of my running theories is that those issues are driving a big and maybe kind of unexpected political realignment — and with the midterms coming up next month, and early voting already underway in a lot of places, the stakes are pretty high right now. So I asked Gov. Pritzker about all that, and he was surprisingly willing to dive right into the absolute existential weeds of what government is even for. You’ll hear him say — and it’s hard to disagree — that some problems are just collective action problems that require the government to do a lot of work. We can’t solve all these problems one at a time, or even one state at a time. It’s a pretty deep conversation, and we really got into it on a lot of issues. And of course, I had to ask him: Are the Bears gonna stay in Illinois? Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Here we go. Gov. JB Pritzker, you’re the governor of Illinois. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks, Nilay. Great to be with you. I am very excited to talk to you. We’re in the heart of midterm season. You are running for reelection. I have to tell you. I have to be very honest with you. I personally feel a lot of pressure in this interview, not only because I’m speaking to a governor, but because I went to school in Chicago. My sister still lives in Chicago. My wife grew up in Illinois. Her entire family is farmers in North Central Illinois. Boy, do I have a list of questions for you. I have to do a good job here. Well, we’re claiming you. Now that I know all that, we’re claiming you. You’re an Illinoisan. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. I don’t know about that. I grew up in Wisconsin. Here’s my first question for you. I’m a die-hard Packers fan. Are you going to let the Bears move to Indiana? That is not our intention. We are, in fact, in discussions with the Bears and the NFL about keeping the Bears either in Chicago or in Arlington Heights, but in Illinois. I’m saying, as a Packers fan, nothing is funnier than the outcome of the Bears moving to Indiana. I just want to put that out there. Openly biased in this case — I own two shares of that stock — but I’m going to make the comparison here. And the reason I started there is not only because I think that’s a funny outcome, although I do, but it feels like we are in the middle of a generational political realignment. I’m sure you feel that, in this election campaign, the idea of big business and how that should interact with the government, and how the government should be able to push back on big business and not give in to big business. All of that feels up for grabs. And the comparison I will make in this specific case is your fellow governor, Gavin Newsom, in California. They sued the Ellison family, Paramount, over the Warner Brothers merger. Paramount threatened to leave. They made a lot of noise about Nashville, Texas, Miami, or wherever you make noise about these days, and it feels like Newsom caved. It feels like he pressured his Attorney General, Rob Bonta, to settle that lawsuit and keep them there. They settled the lawsuit. The next day, the Ellison family is like, “We never… We’re from California. We would never leave.” I see a parallel here with the Bears that is connected to that larger realignment, how government and business should interact. Do you see that parallel? Do you feel that realignment? Well, what I can tell you is we’re pretty tough negotiators in Chicago and Illinois, and that’s really what we’re in the midst of now with the Bears. But I understand your point about realignment. I mean, there is a generational change, and I think it’s also an attitudinal change about protecting taxpayers, protecting people who frankly are among the most vulnerable to all the technology that’s overtaking people’s lives and invading people’s homes. And so I do believe that the government has to be more active now and become a fighter for our people and not just a collaborator with business on everything. I’m a businessman, as you know, before I became governor. But I also know that, for the people of Illinois anyway, my job is to protect the working people of this state who often don’t have anybody protecting them except a government that will stand up for them. So that’s kind of the realignment that I see. And that generational shift, I agree with you. It’s partly a Democratic Party generational shift. Generationally, we’re a little more aggressive. And I’m probably older than the next generation that’s already possibly taking office this November. I’m 61 years old, but I think of myself as having come out of the tech world and as somebody who has been a fighter for progressive values that, yeah, we’ve got to become more aggressive and make sure we’re standing up for our people. There are two places where I see the realignment in particular. One is data centers, one is privacy, and you just see that as a bipartisan backlash to those things. I would actually add a third, which is antitrust broadly. It’s weird if you go into Silicon Valley. David Sacks is retweeting Lina Khan from the Biden administration talking about whether the AI industry needs an antitrust exemption to manage safety. They both agree that these companies don’t need antitrust exemptions. They actually should be more competitive. Again, putting that in the context of regulating these companies, thinking about the dynamic between the government and the biggest companies in the world. I’ll just ask the question, I guess, more directly. Do you think Newsom was right to give in to Paramount, or do you think he should have forced them to make good on that threat to leave? I can’t speak to the Paramount situation well enough to give you an answer, so it would be unfair for me to do so. I can say once again that our orientation today — and I think about the big AI companies and the big social media companies as well — has to be like, wait a minute, too much power in too few hands. Particularly when we talk about AI, where it’s potentially existential, but certainly transformative, which is probably a kind way to say it about the economy, that we’re going to have to get very engaged. Guardrails, of course, on both parts, but also addressing what I think on the AI front is potentially a significant change in employment in the United States. I’m not somebody who is necessarily convinced that we have to see a whole bunch of job loss, but that does feel like that’s the direction this is going. What I’m suggesting is we better be prepared, and we better be protecting people who are going to lose their jobs, or at least it appears they’re going to lose their jobs. And I’ll just give you this thought. If these days 4 percent unemployment is kind of the acceptable near full employment number, I think the problem we’re going to see is — if that’s sort of the level that we’re going to hopefully aim for and stay at — that in very short order, we could end up at 7 percent and have that be the baseline, or maybe 10 percent. And if you think about what’s happened, the upheavals of economies and of governments when you get to 10 percent unemployment in any country. We better be focused on how we’re going to give people the dignity of work and enough income so that they can make a life for themselves when you’re going to put people out of work by virtue of this technology. By the way, much of the benefit of that is going to go to a very, very few people. So we’ve got to wrestle with that and come to a conclusion. I wanted to start with some of the brinksmanship we have seen in the negotiations between, particularly, states and the big companies, because that brinksmanship is real. The threat is we will leave. We just covered, I don’t know, Kevin O’Leary in Utah talking about data centers, and the people of Utah really pushed back against Kevin O’Leary building that data center. But his argument was, “Well, I’m just going to shop around.” This is what states do. They compete with tax incentives and benefits, maybe for data centers, which will put everyone out of a job. They compete for land use rights. You’ve got a rural state with a lot of farms in it. How are you thinking about that dynamic? Do you feel like you’re in competition with the other states, or is this bipartisan realignment creating more of a level playing field where these companies are going to have to actually give something? We are in competition. We just are because it isn’t bipartisan, at least if you ask me. Unless there is a change in the government. I’ll pick on Texas for a second, and there is a chance that you’ll see a new governor in Texas as of November 3rd. In fact, a good chance. But if you look at Texas as it’s run today by a three-term, hoping to be a four-term, Republican governor and a Republican legislature, they have no intention of changing their alignment about incentives. In the state of Illinois, we don’t want to have to do that. I mean, we obviously want to protect the revenue that we’ve got for the state to pay for the things we think are valuable to our people, but we also want to make sure that we’re attracting jobs and not losing jobs. And in a world where South Carolina, Michigan, Texas, Florida — pick your poison. Michigan may be slightly different just because it’s got democratic control, but these are our competitors. When I’m competing to have a company move to Illinois, I’ve got to make sure, first of all, that I’m somewhere in the ballpark when it comes to the incentives, because otherwise we don’t even get considered. And then when I say somewhere in the ballpark, I mean, I want to give away less than more, and then I want to provide whatever other advantages I can that aren’t financial so that I can protect the resources that we have. An example of that is, we like to talk about a kind of white-glove service that we offer to companies. If you’re going to bring a factory here, let’s say, just to give an example, we want to make sure that we’ve got somebody who’s kind of a concierge for your company that’s walking you through each of our departments where you need a permit. It doesn’t mean we’re lowering the standards. It just means, a lot of times, the bureaucracy eats up so much time that it makes it impossible for a company to actually do what they want to do in your state. We try to make sure that if we’re going to attract a large company, with 1,000, 2,000, 3,000 jobs, that we’re at least making it a little easier for them to go through without having to give them massive tax incentives. So that’s the way I think about it. We are in competition. There’s just no doubt about it. Should we be? There’s a lot of discussion about whether we shouldn’t, and maybe at the federal level we should do something about leveling the playing field, but this is the world we’re living in right now. I wanted to ask those questions just to set the baseline. I really do think something is happening. A lot of young people are dissatisfied with the status quo. A lot of people in general are dissatisfied with what big tech companies are trying to do with AI, with the potential for job loss. And the relationship between the people, the government, and those companies seems more fraught than ever, especially as they’re trying to expand their physical infrastructure with data centers, as they all become defense contractors, literally taking our tax dollars to sell weapon systems and collect data for the government. That’s a big swirl. I wanted to start there, but I just want to take one second here and ask you the Decoder questions because I personally think the operation of government is so opaque. It’s very easy to figure out how big companies are run. The CEOs won’t shut up. They’re on podcasts all day long. I think most people have no idea how your job works. So you were elected governor. How is your office set up, and how have you structured the state government of Illinois? Just starting from where I sit, and then, of course, we look at it from a customer service perspective. But starting just at the top, I actually did something that no governor of Illinois has ever done — which is that I created not just one deputy governor. We obviously have a lieutenant governor who’s elected also, but a deputy governor is somebody getting appointed by me to serve under me, to help manage the government with me. What I did was put four deputy governors in place, a general counsel, and my chief of staff. Why is that important? Because what I’ve tried to do is to break down the silos of government. I took all of the health and human services-related departments — that’s the Department of Public Health, the Department of Human Services, the Department of Healthcare and Family Services, everything from health insurance, Medicaid, and public health during the pandemic — and put it all under one deputy governor working directly for me. The idea is that instead of my having, let’s say, 26 direct reports, I’ve got four or five direct reports plus my chief of staff, who each have, let’s say, six or seven departments underneath them. From my perspective, what I wanted to do was make sure that I’m breaking down the silos of government, making these departments that are often building walls, and they don’t want to talk to one another because they’re afraid they might lose jobs in one department to another department, or lose control of a program if they’re talking to one another. That’s the way it used to be. Now we’re like the deputy governor is there to either beat the heads together or at least bring them together so that they will be operating the government more efficiently. Okay, so that’s from the top. From the bottom, which is: how do people who live in Illinois interact with the state government? And obviously, technology is one of the upgrades that’s occurred and made it easier. Illinois, frankly, had not significantly invested in those processes before I became governor, or in the technology that was necessary. And I’ll just give you one example of this: We created something called BEACON, which is designed to address the problem that parents and families have with mental health for children. It turns out that there were seven different ways in which people approached the government to get help, and we weren’t coordinating those, and we weren’t helping to provide all of the resources. I’m talking about outside resources. How do you find a therapist? How do you find a psychiatrist? And how do you pay for those things? Medicaid, if you can’t afford it on your own. But the point is, there’s one door to enter through BEACON that allows you to get access to all of those resources, even if they’re in multiple departments. So that’s just one example. We’re trying to think of this as a customer service operation. It’s one thing to say this is how the org chart looks and another thing to say, this is how you access all the resources of the government that you need. We provide programs that really matter to people. We have a birth equity initiative to reduce maternal mortality, particularly in Black and Brown communities. And free diapers for some people. The problem is, people don’t even know that the programs exist, and how would you ever figure out that the programs exist, especially if you’re a working person who’s working two minimum-wage jobs? You don’t have any time, and you don’t have any money, and you don’t even know how to talk to the government. And so we’re trying to fix all of those problems of the government with the way that we interact with people. It’s funny. It feels like that is one of the bigger opportunities when it comes to AI, just letting the AI navigate a bureaucracy for you and communicate what resources are available. The flip side of that is that people hate AI. They truly dislike it, and it doesn’t feel like that connection has been made — that a lot of these tools can actually just navigate a bureaucracy for you. Are you thinking that should be an investment that you make, that it might be what turns the tide in terms of how people feel about these tools? Yes, but I’m not plunging headlong into it. And I realize that there are probably states that are plunging headlong into it. I mean, the United States government rolled out its AI chatbot to look at webpages across the government. Well, there you go. I guess what I’m trying to do is make sure that… I created something called the AI Cabinet in my government, and that is to essentially bring the experts on AI together with the leaders of my mainstay agencies of state government, so that we’re thinking about privacy, safety, and efficiency. And those things have to be talked about together. You can’t just say we’re going after efficiency and we don’t really care about the other two. So that’s the idea, the AI cabinet. It’s also that, honestly, there are things, as you know, about AI that are dangerous. And so we’ve got our emergency management agency on that AI cabinet. We’ve got our state police on that AI cabinet. And remember, a lot of the people that work in those agencies aren’t particularly proficient at AI or really understand the potential and the potential dangers. That’s why we brought in experts, for example, from the University of Chicago, the University of Illinois, just as two examples of places where we’re drawing expertise. So yeah, there’s a lot to be done. I would say we’re trying to approach it carefully before it gets out of control to a point where we have no way to pull it back in. The other Decoder question I ask everybody is about decisions. You have a big job. You have some constraints in your decision-making process, right? There’s a state legislature, there’s a federal government, you have other agencies in your state. How do you make decisions? What’s your framework? Well, I don’t do it the way Donald Trump does. It’s funny you say it that way. I guess I start with the idea that we have a problem to solve and that decisions have to get made. Are those decisions ones that need to come to the governor? Because you’re right, I only have so much bandwidth. So the question is: which are the most serious ones that can’t be solved by other people, or are unlikely to get the outcomes that I would want by handing them over to other people? And then those automatically come to me. So what I’m making decisions about is kind of the first answer to your question, and then it’s how do I actually make the decisions? For me, I am not one of those people who thinks that I’m right 100 percent of the time. Maybe a good way to describe it, and I’m joking a little bit when I say it, is that I’m 90 percent sure I’m right, but there’s also a 10 percent chance that I’m dead wrong. I want to make sure that I’m getting input and a debate before I actually make the final decision. Someone once told me that the best CEOs are ones that, in their organization, are a little bit below average in terms of their capability and intellect. I’m not saying we want below-average leaders. I’m just saying you’re so good at hiring that you’ve got people in your organization who are really far better than you are at various things that you’re not particularly good at. Maybe knowing what you don’t know and being willing to ask for help is a philosophy that I have. Be willing to ask for help if it’s something you really don’t know. And I’ll be honest, when you become governor of a state, there are a whole lot of topics within the purview of a governor. Making decisions about all those topics, maybe a human being who has super intelligence might be able to do it, but most people don’t start out knowing everything there is to know about public health, public safety, and education. And so you start out with what you know and then try to add expertise to it and then make decisions based upon the best experts debating one another in front of you. At least that’s how I like to do it. Give me an example. Governor Kathy Hochul from New York was on the show. She said in her first week she needed to declare a state of emergency because of a hurricane, and she just didn’t know how, which was very humanizing in its way. Give me an example of when you became governor, and there was something where you just didn’t know. COVID. Sure. I mean, honestly, no one runs for governor thinking there’s going to be a global pandemic. You think you’re going to solve education problems for people or put more money in people’s pockets by raising the minimum wage or whatever, but COVID comes along. And I have to admit, the level of expertise, I don’t think any governor… Well, maybe Josh Green, the doctor who’s the governor of Hawaii, maybe he had a lot to [of expertise] start with — but for the rest of us humans, that was one where we were learning on the job. We were working 18 hours per day. My entire team was all in, and we had to do things like emergency procurement of ventilators and masks, and we had to go outside the box. It’s not like we could just put it through our central management services, look for a contract, or whatever. This was like, I need masks in three days. I’ll tell you a quick story, if you’re interested, about my interaction with Donald Trump at the time because I think it’s interesting, anyway. But I’m not a big fan of Donald Trump, in case you didn’t know. I was one year into office when the COVID pandemic hit, and I had not… I mean, I talked to his administration, but I didn’t talk to him directly. So I picked up the phone and called him, and I said, “Mr. President.” By the way, I wrote a script for myself because I know he likes to be flattered, and I’m not somebody who normally likes to flatter him, but I wrote a script for myself. I saved it; I even have it today. And I said, “Mr. President, you’re a great businessman, but you can understand that paying $8 for an N95 mask that should cost us 75 cents means we’re in a national emergency. We need to be able to get these things and afford them, and I’m competing against all the other states. We need to invoke the Defense Production Act in order to make sure that we’re making enough masks in the United States.” That’s what I told him. And then I said, “But I need masks right now. What can you do for me?” I said, “I need 2 million N95 masks, and I need 4,000 ventilators.” And he never delivered, just so you know, even though he promised that he would deliver. The challenges in COVID were mighty, and the organization that we had to create around it… I had meetings every morning just on this topic, figuring out, okay, how many hospital beds [are available]? We didn’t have a system that would tell us statewide how many hospital beds are available in each region. What happens if you have an outbreak and it really is overtaking some region? What do we do? And so these were all the things we had to learn on the fly. And all I can tell you is, once again, back to hiring great people to have around you, I really felt like I proved that I had done a good job of hiring because the people around me were tremendous. One of whom, by the way, is now running as my lieutenant governor partner in this election. It’s interesting you brought up COVID in the context of our conversation about generational political realignment. I would actually point to COVID as the beginning of a particular realignment around what the government should measure, how much control the government should have over people, and all of that has led, I think, directly into the bipartisan pushback against Flock cameras. The very notion of privacy is not, in my mind, left or right anymore. The CEO of Flock got himself in all kinds of trouble because he kept saying all the people who wanted to ban Flock cameras are criminals, and he would go on MAGA media and say this. I think that position was just rejected. We can see in states around the country that there’s pushback against Flock cameras. I would point to COVID as the beginning of that. The idea that the government could be too intrusive, and in particular, the government should not be able to measure things. “If you don’t test, there won’t be COVID” just became an idea. And the idea that we shouldn’t measure things, or we should tear down our systems of measurement, is a big part of the second Trump administration. But I see that privacy connection very clearly to COVID. In one world, the government coming together to protect its citizens and build a bunch of systems could have gone a very different way. In the one we live in, there’s ferocious pushback to that, on the left and the right in some ways. How do you feel about privacy right now? I know Illinois leads the nation. You’ve got the Biometric Identification Protection Act. Every time I fly to Chicago, I’ve got to push the button at the airport to say that it’s okay to look at my face. That’s one way of going about it. But then you do have, I think, hundreds of Flock cameras in Cook County alone. People have Meta glasses with cameras in them. There’s something happening with privacy that is running right into the aftershocks of COVID and how people feel about government intrusion. How are you finding a way through that balance? Well, and don’t forget AI. Yep. As you’re suggesting. I mean, talk about a collision. This focus on privacy is warranted and long overdue, to be honest with you. I understand what you’re describing about COVID, but I think something that came out of COVID got accelerated, and that was conspiracy theories. Yes. And I’m not suggesting that everything you hear now about the pushback around privacy is a conspiracy theory, but it is easy for these things to spread, and people have misinformation that’s informing them about how these things are used. Having said that, I guess what I think is that we are having to solve multiple problems at the same time, and that AI is coming. Let’s just go to AI for a second. It’s here. I mean, I say it’s coming, but it’s here. It’s not going to stop. We’re not going to become Luddites without any AI. So the question is, in the context of privacy, what guardrails are we putting on AI, and how are we managing it? This idea that the president and David Sacks had, where they got all the companies together and said, “Hey, how about you guys self-police?” That’s not going to work, at least not for protecting people’s privacy. And frankly, it’s not going to provide any safety either because everybody’s going to operate in their own self-interest. It’s one of the reasons why you need a government, in my view. I’m not suggesting the government is any smarter than these companies. But one of the reasons you have any kind of collective action of the government is because, separately, as you know, people operate in their own self-interest. I mean, you could have a Hobbesian world where people are killing each other, and there are no rules about it. So I think we’ve got to use the government as a tool and also be smart within the government. And that’s where the generational change, I think, is hugely important. Use the government as a smarter, less bureaucratic collection of people devoted to protecting the privacy of everyone and making sure that we’re addressing all the other challenges that come from AI. So I guess I’ll just say, I don’t think we’re anywhere near where we need to be, but I will say, if we don’t have a federal government, now I’ve got a lot of… I’m very proud of the things that we’ve done here in Illinois around the AI Safety Measures Act, which is the toughest in the country, the Children’s Social Media Safety Act, and so on. I’m proud of the work we’ve done, but state by state, this is not the way to do this. We’re doing the best we can in the absence of a federal government that is addressing these issues. And when I say federal government, I’m not just pointing at Trump. I’m pointing at Congress. No action on their part means that we’re going at it alone. And right now, I don’t know how many AI safety measure acts have been passed, but it looks like three to me. I mean, it’s New York, California, and Illinois. Maybe you could name a couple of others, but we three were the first. And yet, we’ve got 47 other states. This worries me a great deal. You’re raising issues, and I’d love to tell you I have all the answers. I can tell you what we’re trying to think about is that we are the… People sometimes say that the states are laboratories of democracy. They’re actually laboratories of policy, and we are trying to, at least in Illinois, use ourselves as a laboratory for policy while not creating disadvantage for ourselves. And so that’s a very challenging thing to do, and why we need to change what’s happening at the federal government. Focus on privacy for one second. I understand what you’re saying about AI. I think part of the privacy debate around Flock cameras, for example, is, well, sure, you can have one license plate reader in one intersection. And if the cops had to go there and pull the SD card out of it, drive it back to headquarters, upload it to their Apple IIe, and look at it manually, maybe people would feel one way about it. But those cameras are all networked. They don’t have any access controls really. There are infinite reports of local police chiefs tracking their girlfriends across state lines with these cameras. You add in a system like Palantir, which can synthesize multiple databases and do all kinds of tracking across all kinds of systems. People see that. The turn that is being made is that you can connect a lot of databases of information together, search them without a warrant, and track people across the entire country. You could ban that state by state. You could regulate it city by city, which we’re seeing happen with Flock, and you could maybe have some federal controls around privacy there. None of it’s really happening, but on the ground, people are ferociously pushing back. And that’s the connection I’m making to COVID, conspiracy theories, and how much power the government should have to surveil you and look at you. Something happened in there where people’s attitudes about that really shifted. And I would say one of my core beliefs is that Americans do not like being told what to do. Party politics aside, Americans don’t like being told what to do. Something about that flipped and connected to: we have a network of license plate-reading cameras, and we’re going to tear them down when we see them because there’s something about that that offends us as Americans. Illinois does have privacy laws. I think the last update to the biometric law you did was in 2024, and it has changed again. It’s gotten more vociferously opposed to tracking and surveillance in this country. Do you think you need another update to that privacy law? I think we should be looking at that question every year. I’ll give you an example of it. We passed it, and again, I’m back to AI because I think how you’re describing it was a perfect way to say it. If it was an SD card that they had to go grab and then analyze back at the station, it’d be a different thing. But it’s AI that’s operating these things, and that’s allowing this stuff to move instantaneously and track people. Look, should we be addressing it? Yeah, every year. It’s like the issue of ethics in government. What I mean is, the minute you put an ethics law in place, there’s somebody who’s trying to get around it. I mean, every year, it’s like every law… this is probably true across all of capitalism, maybe. There are always people trying to find a way around the law. Put a tax law in place, and someone’s trying to figure out how to get around it. And I think the point you’re making is that that’s why you need to have a proactive government, less bureaucratically and more aggressively trying to address these things. Are we going to be able to keep up with it? I’ll be honest, I don’t think so. And I also don’t think you can say, “Well, we’re just going to shut it all down” because there are things you’re missing out on. It’s sort of like, and again, I keep going back to AI, but I think a lot about it. My children are 21 and 24. They’re going to live to 100 or 110 years old because AI is going to solve a whole bunch of medical challenges, and already is. There’s a cure now for sickle cell anemia, and people who would otherwise die at 25 or 30 years old are going to live full lives. This is going to happen across the board in cancer and everything else. And so there’s all good in there, and then there’s the bad. So I know what you’re saying. I guess all I can tell you is I’m a believer that we can progressively — I don’t mean that in a political fashion — address these challenges. In Illinois, we passed a law that disallows the use of AI in therapy for people because we think too much information gets collected, not enough humanity in the process, and we think that it should have humanity in it. Again, we’re not trying to shut it down across the board, but we’re going to have to see how it gets used and where it’s improper. And I know that sounds imperfect because the technology is moving so fast that the idea that we’re going to be able to keep up with all the ways in which someone’s privacy could be breached seems very difficult, but I don’t know any other way to do it. That’s why you have a government, and maybe in the end we’re going to have this competing use of things like AI, where AI is monitoring AI, and AI that’s kind of privacy-friendly or focused on privacy is going to be monitoring the AI that’s not. But again, I know you don’t want to just talk about AI. I am concerned. This issue of privacy has been around for a long time. You’ve been talking about it, I’m sure; I’ve been talking about it since before AI. This is like everybody giving over their personal information in exchange for access to something. And that was happening for a while, and then we’re all getting ads that are personalized to us based on stuff that we’ve essentially given up privacy for. No, it’s funny. People believe, and we can write as many stories as we want about how your iPhone is not actually listening to you, but the ad tracking is so good that everyone believes that their iPhones are listening to them. The next turn is that it is now technologically feasible for these systems to listen to you all the time. And I can’t fall back on the idea that it’s cheaper for them to do the ad tracking when you hit I accept than to listen to you all the time, which was, for a decade, the right answer. The economically correct answer was that ad tracking was cheaper than listening to you all the time. That might be very different in the future. There are already devices that we cover here at The Verge that purport to listen to you all the time and turn that into some actionable data. And it feels to me like the tech industry is trying to drive a truck through our privacy law, through our lack of AI regulations, through an entire system of governance that is designed for the pre-AI era. The notion that you don’t have privacy in public worked really well when everyone didn’t have a cell phone that could connect to the cloud and instantly search every photo all at once, all the time, and do facial recognition. We live in that world now. I would say the public sentiment towards the idea that you don’t have privacy in public places has turned. They don’t like the Meta glasses. They call them pervert glasses for a reason. And somewhere in there is, well, the federal government should pass privacy law. It is a failure of imagination in the United States. We don’t have federal privacy law. And then somewhere in there is the notion that the states are laboratories of democracy and policy. It is amazing, by the way, how often on this tech and business show, Thomas Hobbes comes up and the very notion that the government is there to serve as an extension of us solving collective action problems. It comes up over and over again because I think the tech industry does not want to respect that dynamic. This is why I started with that relationship between government and business, and the pushback and the negotiation, because here it feels like the tech industry is in a bubble of its own making. Truly, in a media bubble of its own making. And then all of the polling is, well, we hate AI. In particular, young people hate AI. And then all of the action is around data centers where NIMBYism, the most American of policy levers, is being pulled to keep these data centers out of communities. And that’s one way to stop AI. You just pulled back on data center tax incentives in July. You’re pushing the state legislature to adopt a suite of guarantees on reforms for new construction. Do you think data centers and the pushback on data centers is an effective route towards AI regulation? No, I don’t. I think it’s an effective route toward data center regulation. I know that people have conflated and put together their opposition to data centers with their opposition to AI. And a lot of people can’t describe why they’re opposed to one or the other because they’re conflated with one another. But I can say that — I mean, at least our aim is focused on the idea, and people really feel this, right, and there’s real data to back this up — the data centers themselves put aside what they’re doing inside a data center. The data centers and what’s happening are eating up the available electricity, and that’s causing your electric bill to go up. At least that’s how everybody feels. There are a lot of things that we should have been doing in many years gone by to get to a point where electricity bills shouldn’t have to go up now. And that has to do with building out the grid. It’s a world where regulation and cross-border challenges have made it nearly impossible for a lot of the grid to get built the way that it should have. We produce a lot more electricity in the United States than we use, but we just don’t transport it well enough, and we would have a lot more available if we transported it better. Okay, but even if you think that can’t happen efficiently, we need to build more capacity on the grid. My only point is the opposition to data centers is, in part, a result of the economic situation that’s happening right now in the country, where electric bills, gas, rent, everything has gone up. Your electric bill shows up every month, and it continues to go up, and people kind of scratch their heads and say, “Who am I paying for?” This is happening, and this is particular to Illinois. We’re not going to have a whole discussion about energy policy, but I could just say this: We produce more nuclear power in the state of Illinois than any other state. Roughly 53 or 54 percent of our electricity comes from nuclear power, and we’re a net electricity exporter. So we have an excess in Illinois, but our bills are going up, and that’s because of the methodology of the regional transmission organizations. Again, not to get into all the details of it, but essentially, if Ohio decides to build a hyperscale data center, our bills in Illinois are affected, and that’s shocking to people who live in Illinois. But what they know is they don’t want their bill to go up, so they don’t want another data center nearby — even though the one in Ohio is actually causing the problem, even if you choose to oppose data centers. So this is a challenge. I think there’s a lot of information that needs to be spread. But most of all, we just need a whole lot more capacity and a whole lot more grid that will, I think, subside some of the concern about data centers. To your point, privacy is, I think, more related to AI than data centers. And it’s not just AI, but the way AI is used. So we’re going to have a lot of opposition. You make an excellent point. I think this feeling of being out of control — you are not in control of your environment anymore — that’s the thing that is causing anxiety. I want to go back to something really important that I was saying earlier. We need better people running for public office. We need smarter policy development in government. And part of that is a generational shift that’s needed and a better understanding. We have people who are serving in the United States Senate who have no idea. Was it the Secretary of Education, Trump’s Secretary of Education, who called it A1? I mean, because we’ve got older people who don’t have any exposure who are making policy theoretically on these things, and it should disturb us all. It’s one of the reasons we’ve got to advance the cause of better people and better systems in government. We are on the cusp of an election. There might be a new Congress. There might be new leadership in Congress. There are a bunch of old Democrats too. In fact, I could probably point directly to Joe Biden’s age in the last election as the reason that he lost. Do you think that you need a wholesale change of leadership of the older Democrats as well? You said, “Do we need a wholesale change?” I mean, I can tell you that I don’t think we should be telling — Well, now I live in New York. I’ll just ask you, do you think Chuck Schumer should be the Senate majority leader if the Democrats take the Senate? That’s a decision people in the Senate are going to make. I have no influence over it. I can tell you this: I am opposed to term limits because I think that you should have all the choices. You’re a voter. If you want to vote for the 75-year-old, I mean, go ahead. I’m just suggesting that a great case could be made for the 45-year-old who’s just as smart as the 75-year-old was when he was 45, or maybe is now, but has a modern look at the issues around AI privacy, everything else we’re discussing, and a more aggressive view of how we ought to be reining in big corporations in their invasion of our lives. But I think people ought to make their own choices. I mean, for us to say, “Well, we should have an age limit. You’re 70, that’s it, you’re out.” I think that belies who we are as a democracy. Well, you convinced me. I’m 46. I’m announcing my run for president here with you, Governor. That was a rousing speech. Listen, I would vote for you in a second if the choice was you and Donald Trump. A low bar, but I’m glad I crossed it. Let me tie two ideas together at the end. We’ve talked a lot about AI regulation. You mentioned social media regulation a little bit earlier in this conversation. I know that Illinois has a social media law. You have a bell-to-bell ban on phones in schools for kids. I’m just going to pick on Mark Zuckerberg. It’s easy to pick on Mark Zuckerberg. If you look at how he talks about social media regulation, he basically describes the tragedy of the commons. You signed the landmark settlement with him. I think Illinois is due to get $750 or $760 million out of that settlement. And a big part of it is that TikTok and YouTube have to agree to the same terms, and then Meta will pay the rest of the money. And Zuckerberg very clearly has said that’s because if Instagram falls back on engagement bait and TikTok doesn’t, the kids will just use TikTok. And so the government has to get everyone to agree. I will tell you that Neal Mohan, the CEO of YouTube, does not agree. He’s not going to sign onto this. That’s one whole fight. Look at how Mark Zuckerberg talks about AI regulation. There’s none of that dynamic at all. He’s like, “It should be a free-for-all. We’ll all compete. If it’s not safe, the market will tell us. We’ll be fine.” And in my mind, these ideas are at total odds with each other. In the market where he makes all the money, the government has to step in and stop him from hurting kids because apparently there’s no market demand for safe social media. And in the market where the AI CEOs are telling us they might kill us all if we don’t stop them, it’s a free-for-all, and the market will tell us if they accidentally kill everybody. How do you reconcile those things? Are you just happy that you got the social media case done after a decade of failing to regulate social media, or do you think you can solve AI with regulation this time instead of letting it just cook? Look, I’m an optimist at heart, so I’m not going to suggest to you that I absolutely know that we can solve all the problems that we’re now facing, but I don’t know what else we can do. Other than, again, progressively making sure that we’re trying to address each of these things, trying to anticipate them to the extent we can. Can we be faster than AI is developing? I don’t know. But we can’t stop trying. I know that. And I would suggest to you that my optimism is founded because I think the vast majority of people want what you’re describing, which is reining it in. And again, without destroying companies. I don’t think we’re all trying to do that. What we’re trying to do is stop the invasion into our home, stop the invasion into our children’s lives. I do think we can do that, but that’s because we’ve solved a whole lot of huge problems. That’s kind of like my answer to: is AI potentially existential? The answer, of course, is yes. And can we solve it? I don’t know. Nuclear weapons… I mean, just to give something of an analogy to something else. I mean, nuclear weapons are still hanging over us as a danger to humanity. And so far anyway, we’ve managed not to blow up the world. I don’t know whether that gives you any optimism, but it does to me. We, as a country, can figure out how we want to rein it in here. That we, as a country, can work with our allies to figure out how we want to collectively try to rein it in. And then we have enemies in the world and competitors in the world, and we’ve got to figure out how we’re going to… Maybe it’s mutually assured destruction, like it was with nuclear weapons, but these are all things we’re going to have to work on, and work on fast. And it’s scary because someone analogized this to… I mean, think about the early 1950s when every kid had to learn that if there was a nuclear blast, an atomic bomb that went off, get under your desk. That wouldn’t have been very effective. But the point is, people lived with the idea that a terrible nuclear holocaust could occur with a nuclear explosion. And so I think we’re heading into that world again with AI. I hope I didn’t stray too much from your question, but — Let me ask you this, and it’s a little bit of a wild card here at the end. We cover this industry so closely here, and the big difference with nuclear weapons is that there weren’t five companies building bleeding-edge nuclear weapons in private capacity, led by five guys who all hated each other. But that’s the dynamic of the AI industry. They all truly hate each other, and they’re all trying to make as much money as they can as fast as they can. And then some of them think the AI is alive. If you ask Anthropic, and we’ve done this, “Is Claude alive?” They don’t say no. They will argue with you about the definition of alive and suggest that, to them, alive means having a biological component and Claude doesn’t have that, but it might be conscious. There’s a race to build AGI in the industry. Some people truly believe they’re building alien minds that have a different kind of consciousness. I’m not sure any government at any level has ever had to regulate that, or has ever come up against an industry that is religious about the fact that it might be building the next kind of intelligence. Where do you stand? Do you think that they’re building a next kind of consciousness that stands alongside humans, or do you think that this is normal technology as some others do? Boy, that is really another podcast for us, but I’ll just say this one thing: I just want to disagree with you for a second. Nobody could ever imagine a nuclear weapon either. And… But the government built nuclear weapons. It wasn’t — I understand. I’m not suggesting it’s the same. I’m suggesting it’s so new at the time that figuring out how you’re going to rein it in… Because remember, it’s not just one government, and the same thing with AI. It’s not just those five guys either. I mean, it’s like there’s somebody in China. Maybe five of those. I don’t know, and somebody in Europe or whatever. You could say we’re ahead, or they’re ahead. I don’t know. But all I’m saying is, yeah, this is a proliferated situation and it’s not government-controlled. One hundred percent, you’re right; it’s not like nuclear weapons in that sense. But it is like nuclear weapons in the sense that nobody’s ever seen it before. It’s a complete mystery to start with. How are we going to rein it in? I mean, nobody thought Russia was going to get the bomb, and they got it. We’ve figured out somehow how to deal with it. Again, you’ve got to be an optimist to believe we can end up with the right solution here. I don’t know that we have the answer to “how do we rein it in?” I will say, though, that if we had the power to create it, we have the power, in my view, to rein it in. Is it conscious? You’re asking a deep question. Have you felt the AGI? I mean, do you think it’s conscious? Because I understand why people think it might have consciousness or it’s going to be conscious. But I think that’s why the ethicists and technologists need to be involved. And especially, in my view, the government’s got to be involved because how else are you going to rein in the five guys and the companies that have developed this? There is no other way. I will tell you, I don’t think it’s conscious. And every now and again, you have an experience where it’s blindingly clear why other people believe that. When you watch a reasoning model take 90 steps over an hour and arrive at a conclusion, it’s impressive, and you can see why people believe that. I do not, and I have a lot of reasons for that. It just occurs to me that if you set out to regulate a technology like this, if you believe one thing, you would maybe go down one path. And if you believe that you were building a consciousness, you might go down another. Again, the whole industry itself does not agree on this. Jensen Huang and Dario Amodei do not agree on whether it’s alive. Jensen just wants to sell a bunch of chips, and he will happily tell you it’s just technology and you can control it. I think Dario thinks he’s building AGI, and that’s a different… There’s a whole reason he proposes different kinds of regulatory structures there. I’m just asking you, have you felt the AGI? Do you think it’s one path or the other? I’m not going to give you a satisfactory yes or no. I mean, I haven’t felt it. I guess that’s what I’m… My basic answer is I haven’t felt it. Governor Pritzker, this was very fun. Thank you for indulging this last existential loop of a question. You’re going to have to come back to Decoder soon. I would like to do that. Thanks, Nilay. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

items.summary: Antibody patterns in the blood may help doctors identify people at risk so they can be treated earlier, research shows Patterns of antibodies in people’s blood could predict the onset of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) a decade before diagnosis, according to research that raises hopes for catching the condition early. Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, the two main forms of IBD, are typically treated only after symptoms appear, when the gut has already been damaged. items.title: The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information | Editorial
items.summary: In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics Is there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks since a worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases. It is this uncertainty that has the World Health Organization (WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future. items.title: Margaret Hamilton obituary
items.summary: Pioneering software engineer whose work was critical to the Apollo moon landings Apollo was a bold, innovative project. It tested the boundaries of technology and human achievement, and took people to the moon. However, one thing it failed to challenge was the prevailing hierarchy. Nearly everyone involved in Nasa’s space programme in the 1960s was male and white. If you weren’t, you needed to be exceptional at what you did. Margaret Hamilton, who has died aged 90, was one of those exceptional people. Without her input, sending spacecraft into lunar orbit, and putting Neil Armstrong and his successors on to the surface of the moon, might have been impossible. Continue reading...

articles.title: 中 돌아가는 쌍둥이 판다, 12월 11일 마지막 공개
articles.snippet: 12월 중국으로 돌아가야 하는 에버랜드 쌍둥이 판다(사진) 루이바오와 후이바오를 국내에서 만날 수 있는 마지막 날이 잠정적으로 12월 11일로 정해졌다. 삼성물산 리조트 부문 에버랜드는 루이바오와 후이바오의 국제 이동을 위한 야생동물 사전 검역을 11월 13일 시작한다고 19일 밝혔다. 에버랜드 측은 “검역 절차에 들어가더라도 쌍둥이 판다는 관람객과 제한적 만남을 가질 수 있을 예정”이라며 “판다 세컨드 하우스는 외부와 완전히 차단된 실내 방사 시설이기 때문”이라고 설명했다. 다만 마지막 공개일을 포함한 관람 일정은 달라질 수 있다. 에버랜드는 두 판다의 건강 상태와 검역 진행 상황, 이송 준비 등을 살펴 공개 시간과 관람 방식을 조정할 방침이다. 쌍둥이 판다의 최종적인 중국 이송 날짜와 이동 장소 역시 기온과 현지 여건을 검토한 뒤 확정될 예정이다. 이들 판다는 2023년 7월 엄마 아이바오와 아빠 러바오 사이에서 태어난 국내 첫 쌍둥이 판다 자매로 화제를 낳았다.

articles.title: 한전 “송변전설비 매년 10조 필요” 투자 재원 놓고 논란

articles.title: 中 돌아가는 쌍둥이 판다, 12월 11일 마지막 공개
articles.snippet: 12월 중국으로 돌아가야 하는 에버랜드 쌍둥이 판다(사진) 루이바오와 후이바오를 국내에서 만날 수 있는 마지막 날이 잠정적으로 12월 11일로 정해졌다. 삼성물산 리조트 부문 에버랜드는 루이바오와 후이바오의 국제 이동을 위한 야생동물 사전 검역을 11월 13일 시작한다고 19일 밝혔다. 에버랜드 측은 “검역 절차에 들어가더라도 쌍둥이 판다는 관람객과 제한적 만남을 가질 수 있을 예정”이라며 “판다 세컨드 하우스는 외부와 완전히 차단된 실내 방사 시설이기 때문”이라고 설명했다. 다만 마지막 공개일을 포함한 관람 일정은 달라질 수 있다. 에버랜드는 두 판다의 건강 상태와 검역 진행 상황, 이송 준비 등을 살펴 공개 시간과 관람 방식을 조정할 방침이다. 쌍둥이 판다의 최종적인 중국 이송 날짜와 이동 장소 역시 기온과 현지 여건을 검토한 뒤 확정될 예정이다. 이들 판다는 2023년 7월 엄마 아이바오와 아빠 러바오 사이에서 태어난 국내 첫 쌍둥이 판다 자매로 화제를 낳았다.

articles.snippet: “스스로 작전할 수 있는지 확인하고 넘겨주겠다는 게 고맙긴 한데 우리 스스로 해야 할 일이 아닌가 생각한다.” 이재명 대통령은 19일 기자간담회에서 전시작전통제권(전작권)의 신속한 전환을 강조하며 이같이 말했다. 정부의 전작권 조기 전환 추진에 미국이 ‘조건’ 충족을 강조하며 한미 간 이견이 본격화된 가운데 군사주권과 자주국방 차원에서 조기 전환의 당위성을 강조한 것. 전작권 전환 시 고도화된 북핵·미사일 위협에 대응이 약화될 수 있다는 우려에 대해선 “(북핵은) 최후 방어 무기에 해당한다”고 말했다. 일각에선 북핵을 ‘체제 방어용’으로 규정하면서 핵 불균형에 대한 대응 필요성을 평가절하한 것 아니냐는 지적이 나온다.● “북핵은 최후 방어 무기” 이 대통령은 이날 전작권 관련 질의에 “대한민국은 자주적인 독립국가”라며 “국가로서의 최소한의 요건, 군사 주권을 갖추기 위해 반드시 신속하게 돌려받아야 한다”고 말했다. 특히 “전작권은 ‘전환’ 표현을 썼는데 환수, 환원해야 한다고

articles.title: 李 “지배경영권 남용 등에 증시 저평가” 기업에 화살
articles.snippet: 이재명 대통령이 최근 이어진 국내 증시 하락세에 대해 “(주가가) 많이 오르면 조정이 불가피하다”면서도 “다만 대한민국 주식시장은 매우 저평가된 게 사실”이라고 말했다. 그 이유로 기업 지배경영권 남용을 언급하며 추가 대책을 예고했다. 이 대통령은 19일 청와대 춘추관에서 기자단과 만나 최근 코스피 하락으로 국민연금이 보유한 국내 주식 평가액이 크게 줄었다는 질문을 받고 “주식시장이 부동산시장이랑 비슷하지만 어느 일방향으로 끝까지 갈 수 없다”며 이같이 말했다. “과거와 다르게 정부가 금융시장, 증권시장에 직접 개입하기 어렵고, 바람직하지도 않다”고도 했다. 국내 주식시장이 저평가된 이유로 이 대통령은 “지배경영구조, 시장의 투명성, 대한민국의 지정학적 위상, 산업경제 정책의 불확실성” 등을 꼽았다. 그러면서 “이 중 정책 불확실성은 많이 개선됐을 것”이라며 “남아 있는 게 시장에 대한 불신”이라고 설명했다. 최근 글로벌 반도체 기업의 주가가 일제히 내림세인 가운데 코스피

articles.title: 李 “SNS 없었으면 나도 없다… 목숨줄-숨구멍”
articles.snippet: 이재명 대통령은 19일 소셜네트워크서비스(SNS) 게시글이 크게 늘어난 데 대해 “SNS가 없었으면 이재명 대통령이 있었을까. 과연 경기도지사가 되고 그 후에 집중된 포화 속에서 살아남을 수 있었을까”라고 말했다. 국무회의 생중계를 줄여야 한다는 지적에 대해선 “하급 공무원도 아닌 일국의 장관인데 그걸 누가 지켜보고 있기 때문에 반박할 수 없다는 건 바람직하지 않다”고 일축했다. 이 대통령은 이날 “(SNS는) 저의 장점이라고 생각한다”며 “제가 목숨줄이라고 표현했다”고 말했다. 이어 “정치하는 분들에게도 국민과의 직접 소통을 늘려라, SNS를 많이 하라고 한다”며 “어느 순간에 본인을 살릴 숨구멍은 SNS”라고 강조했다. ‘목숨줄’과 ‘숨구멍’에 비유하며 SNS 활동을 이어가겠다는 뜻을 분명히 한 것이다. 이 대통령은 일부 SNS 게시글이 대통령의 권위를 떨어뜨린다는 비판이 나온 데 대해선 “옛날에 임금도 밤에 몰래 평민 복장하고 뒷골목 주막집 가서 뭔 얘기 하나 들어봤다”고

articles.snippet: 도널드 트럼프 미국 대통령이 19일(현지 시간) 중국 선전에서 11월 열리는 아시아태평양경제협력체(APEC) 정상회의 참석을 계기로 김정은 북한 국무위원장과 만날 가능성에 대해 “모르겠다”고 밝혔다.트럼프 대통령은 이날 백악관에서 기자들과 만난 자리에서 ‘다음 달 중국에서 북한 지도자와 만날 수 있다고 생각하나’라는 질의에 “나도 모르겠다”고 답했다. 그러면서 “누가 회담을 요청하고 있는지도 확실하지 않다(I’m not sure that anybody’s asking for a meeting)”고 덧붙였다.다만 그는 “나는 김정은 위원장과 아주 잘 지내고 있다(but my relationship with Kim Jong Un is very good)”며 김 위원장과의 친분이 여전히 두텁다고 주장했다. 트럼프 대통령의 이날 발언에 대해 불과 1주일 전과는 미묘한 온도차를 보이고 있는 평가가 나온다. 그는 12일(현지 시간) 백악관에서 ‘다음 달 아시아 방문 중 김 위원장과 만날

articles.title: 李 “전작권 맡겨놓고 방치할 상황 아냐… 반드시 조기 환수”

articles.title: 피자 속에 김치… 글로벌 외식 브랜드 뚫은 ‘K푸드’
articles.snippet: ‘코리안 피자’, ‘고추장 치킨’, ‘파김치 크림치즈 베이글’…. 글로벌 외식 브랜드들 사이에서 김치와 고추장 등 한국 식재료를 접목한 신메뉴들이 쏟아지고 있다. 한국 시장이 타깃이 아니라 폴란드, 인도, 미국 등 해외 시장이 출시 대상이다. 세계적으로 K푸드의 인기가 높아지고 외식 수요 위축으로 신메뉴 출시 경쟁이 치열해지면서 한국의 맛이 색다른 차별화의 핵심 전략으로 자리 잡은 것이란 분석이 나온다.● 피자부터 셰이크까지… 김치·고추장 접목19일 글로벌 식품업계에 따르면 폴란드 피자헛은 지난달 1일부터 다음 달 2일까지 한국 음식에서 영감을 받은 ‘코리안 피자’ 4종을 한정 판매한다. 대표 제품인 ‘K-팝 피자’는 고추장을 넣은 마늘 소스로 맛을 낸 면에 베이컨과 참깨를 올린 메뉴다. 치킨너겟과 옥수수에 고추장 소스를 곁들인 ‘K-소울 피자’와 김치와 모차렐라 치즈를 조합한 ‘K-바이브 피자’도 함께 내놨다. 현지 소비자들에게 익숙한 피자에 고추장과 김치 등 한국 대표 식재

articles.snippet: 이찬진 금융감독원장이 단일종목 레버리지 상장지수펀드(ETF)의 상장 일정을 맞추기 위해 심사를 빨리 진행한 측면이 있다고 밝혔다. 금융 당국이 고위험 상품인 단일종목 레버리지 상품의 상장 여부를 졸속으로 심사하는 바람에 2조 원이 넘는 투자 손실을 초래했다는 비판을 피하기 어려울 것으로 보인다. 19일 국회 정무위원회 금감원 국감에서 이 원장은 “4월 중순 금융위원회에서 (단일종목 레버리지) 상장 일정을 정책적으로 발표한 게 있다”면서 “그 일정을 맞추기 위해 심사를 빨리 한 부분이 있다”고 말했다. 단일종목 레버리지 상품은 올해 5월 27일 16개 종목이 상장됐다.● 단일종목 레버리지, 일반 ETF의 절반 만에 이뤄져 국민의힘 박대출 의원은 통상 ETF 종목 상장 시 한국거래소 예비 심사와 금감원 증권신고서 심사 등 2단계를 거치는데, 단일종목 레버리지는 거래소 예비 심사가 끝나기도 전에 금감원이 심사했다고 지적했다. 이 영향으로 ETF 상장 심사가 평균 62일, 대표 지수형

articles.title: 소방관 조문 김민석 차량, ‘응급환자 구역’ 주차 논란
articles.snippet: 더불어민주당 김민석 대표가 탑승한 차량이 18일 순직 소방관 조문 당시 응급환자 전용 주차구역에 주차한 사실이 알려지며 논란이 일었다. 민주당은 “운전자가 해당 주차 공간이 응급환자 전용 구간임을 인지하지 못했다”고 사과했다. 당 대표 비서실장인 김태선 의원은 19일 페이스북에 “순직 소방관 조문 당시 응급환자 전용 주차구역에 주차된 차량은 저희 의원실 차량”이라며 “국민 여러분께 심려를 끼쳐드린 점 진심으로 사과드리며 다시는 이런 일이 없도록 각별히 주의하겠다”고 밝혔다. 김 대표는 전날 오후 8시 50분경 경기 부천시 순천향대 부천병원 장례식장에 마련된 고 김진석 소방위의 빈소를 찾아 조문했는데, 당시 김 대표를 병원 입구에 내려준 차량은 응급환자 전용 구역에 주차했다. 민주당 신현영 대변인은 “해당 차량은 병원에 도착해 당 대표와 비서실장이 내린 후 병원 관계자의 안내로 해당 구역에 주차했다”며 “주차 시간 30분도 안 되는 상황에서 차량은 곧바로 병원 지하 주차장으로 이동

articles.title: [단독]전작권 전환 서두르면서…대북 감시전력 툭하면 고장
articles.snippet: 정부가 전시작전통제권 전환에 속도를 내는 가운데 우리 군 핵심 대북 감시·정찰전력의 가동률이 낮아진 것으로 나타났다. 북한 탄도미사일을 탐지하는 조기경보레이더는 낙뢰 고장 뒤 복구에 약 9개월이 걸리면서 지난해와 올해 가동률이 예년보다 크게 떨어졌다. 공중조기경보통제기 E-737(피스아이)과 유인 정찰기 RF-16(새매)의 올해 가동률도 각각 60%대에 그쳤다. 한국군의 연합방위 주도에 필수적인 감시·정찰자산의 안정적 운용부터 뒷받침돼야 한다는 지적이 나온다.● 北 탄도탄 탐지 레이더, 낙뢰에 277일 가동 중단19일 국회 국방위원회 소속 국민의힘 한기호 의원실이 공군에서 받은 자료에 따르면 탄도탄조기경보레이더(그린파인)의 가동률은 2022∼2024년 99%에서 지난해 84.6%, 올해 1∼8월 82.8%로 하락했다. 탄도탄조기경보레이더는 북한이 쏜 탄도미사일을 조기에 탐지·추적해 요격 대응의 ‘골든타임’을 확보하는 한국형미사일방어체계(KAMD)의 핵심 장비다.해당 장비의 가동

articles.title: 北 김여정 또 적반하장 “대남 확성기 재개 검토”
articles.snippet: 김여정 북한 노동당 총무부장이 19일 “대한국 확성기 방송을 재개하는 문제를 검토하고 있다”고 말했다. 비무장지대(DMZ) 지뢰 폭발 사건에도 정부가 대북 확성기 방송 재개에 거리를 둔 가운데, 북한군의 군사분계선(MDL) 침범에 대한 우리 군의 경고 사격에 적반하장식 공세에 나선 것이다. 김정은 북한 국무위원장의 여동생인 김여정은 이날 담화에서 “지금 남부 국경의 상황은 매우 불안정하다”며 “(한국군이) 우리 인원들이 ‘월선’하였다고 근거 없는 트집을 걸면서 자동보총과 대구경기관총으로 경고사격을 가하고 있다”고 주장했다. 이어 “무모한 객기는 분명 엄청난 정세 위기를 확대시키며 커다란 재앙을 스스로 불러오게 될 것”이라며 “우리 군사 지도부는 전술적 타격 수단들을 전 남부 국경선 부근에 증강 배치하는 문제와 대한국 확성기 방송을 재개하는 문제를 검토하고 있다”고 했다. articles.title: 李 “전작권은 국가 최소한의 요건… 맡겨놓고 방치할 상황 아냐”
articles.snippet: “스스로 작전할 수 있는지 확인하고 넘겨주겠다는 게 고맙긴 한데 우리 스스로 해야 할 일이 아닌가 생각한다.” 이재명 대통령은 19일 기자간담회에서 전시작전통제권(전작권)의 신속한 전환을 강조하며 이같이 말했다. 정부의 전작권 조기 전환 추진에 미국이 ‘조건’ 충족을 강조하며 한미 간 이견이 본격화된 가운데 군사주권과 자주국방 차원에서 조기 전환의 당위성을 강조한 것. 전작권 전환 시 고도화된 북핵·미사일 위협에 대응이 약화될 수 있다는 우려에 대해선 “(북핵은) 최후 방어 무기에 해당한다”고 말했다. 일각에선 북핵을 ‘체제 방어용’으로 규정하면서 핵 불균형에 대한 대응 필요성을 평가절하한 것 아니냐는 지적이 나온다.● “북핵은 최후 방어 무기” 이 대통령은 이날 전작권 관련 질의에 “대한민국은 자주적인 독립국가”라며 “국가로서의 최소한의 요건, 군사 주권을 갖추기 위해 반드시 신속하게 돌려받아야 한다”고 말했다. 특히 “전작권은 ‘전환’ 표현을 썼는데 환수, 환원해야 한다고

articles.title: 李 “지배경영권 남용 등에 증시 저평가” 기업에 화살
articles.snippet: 이재명 대통령이 최근 이어진 국내 증시 하락세에 대해 “(주가가) 많이 오르면 조정이 불가피하다”면서도 “다만 대한민국 주식시장은 매우 저평가된 게 사실”이라고 말했다. 그 이유로 기업 지배경영권 남용을 언급하며 추가 대책을 예고했다. 이 대통령은 19일 청와대 춘추관에서 기자단과 만나 최근 코스피 하락으로 국민연금이 보유한 국내 주식 평가액이 크게 줄었다는 질문을 받고 “주식시장이 부동산시장이랑 비슷하지만 어느 일방향으로 끝까지 갈 수 없다”며 이같이 말했다. “과거와 다르게 정부가 금융시장, 증권시장에 직접 개입하기 어렵고, 바람직하지도 않다”고도 했다. 국내 주식시장이 저평가된 이유로 이 대통령은 “지배경영구조, 시장의 투명성, 대한민국의 지정학적 위상, 산업경제 정책의 불확실성” 등을 꼽았다. 그러면서 “이 중 정책 불확실성은 많이 개선됐을 것”이라며 “남아 있는 게 시장에 대한 불신”이라고 설명했다. 최근 글로벌 반도체 기업의 주가가 일제히 내림세인 가운데 코스피

articles.title: 재외동포청 3년 만에 세종으로? 인천 與野 모두 반발
articles.snippet: 2023년 인천에 둥지를 틀고 출범한 외교부 산하 재외동포청이 3년 만에 정부 공공기관 이전 대상에 포함되면서 지역사회가 반발하고 있다. 시민단체와 야당뿐 아니라 여당인 더불어민주당 인천시당도 이전 계획 재검토를 요구하면서 인천 잔류를 촉구하는 목소리가 커지고 있다.● 재외동포청 내년 세종 이전 추진에 반발 확산 행정안전부는 13일 재외동포청 세종 이전 등의 내용을 담은 ‘2차 중앙행정기관 이전’ 세부 계획을 발표했다. 인천에 있는 재외동포청은 내년 상반기 우선 이전 추진 대상에 이름을 올렸다. 재외동포청은 서울과 제주 광주 등 여러 지역의 치열한 유치전 끝에 2023년 6월 인천에 자리를 잡고 출범했다. 당시 외교부는 재외동포들의 편의성과 접근성이 좋고, 지방균형발전을 이끌 수 있다며 인천을 본청 소재지로 정했다. 하지만 출범 3년 만에 세종 이전이 추진되면서 지역 내 반발이 커지고 있다. 재외동포청은 앞서 올해 초 비싼 청사 임차료 등을 이유로 서울 이전을 검토했다가

articles.title: 세계 첨단 교통기술, 강릉에 다 모였다
articles.snippet: ‘교통올림픽’으로 불리는 ‘지능형교통체계(ITS) 세계총회’가 19일 강원 강릉시 올림픽파크 일원에서 개막했다. 강릉시와 국토교통부가 공동 주최하는 이번 총회는 ‘이동성을 넘어 하나되는 세계(Beyond Mobility, Connected World)’를 주제로 5일 동안 열린다. 428개 부스 규모의 첨단 기술 전시회, 193개 학술 세션, 최첨단 ITS 기술 시연 및 시찰 프로그램이 이어진다. 전 세계 90여 개국 전문가와 기업인 등 6만여 명이 참여할 것으로 예상된다. 참가자들은 자율주행, 인공지능(AI), 수요응답형 교통(DRT), 드론, 도심항공교통(UAM), 공간정보 등 첨단 기술이 융합된 미래모빌리티 발전 방향을 공유하고 글로벌 교통 문제 해결을 위한 국제적 협력 방안을 논의한다. 총회는 개막 첫날부터 열기가 뜨거웠다. 강릉 스피드스케이팅경기장에 마련된 전시장은 최첨단 미래 기술을 확인하려는 국내외 관람객들의 발길이 끊이지 않았다. 올림픽파크 야외광장에 조성된 부대

articles.snippet: 이찬진 금융감독원장이 단일종목 레버리지 상장지수펀드(ETF)의 상장 일정을 맞추기 위해 심사를 빨리 진행한 측면이 있다고 밝혔다. 금융 당국이 고위험 상품인 단일종목 레버리지 상품의 상장 여부를 졸속으로 심사하는 바람에 2조 원이 넘는 투자 손실을 초래했다는 비판을 피하기 어려울 것으로 보인다. 19일 국회 정무위원회 금감원 국감에서 이 원장은 “4월 중순 금융위원회에서 (단일종목 레버리지) 상장 일정을 정책적으로 발표한 게 있다”면서 “그 일정을 맞추기 위해 심사를 빨리 한 부분이 있다”고 말했다. 단일종목 레버리지 상품은 올해 5월 27일 16개 종목이 상장됐다.● 단일종목 레버리지, 일반 ETF의 절반 만에 이뤄져 국민의힘 박대출 의원은 통상 ETF 종목 상장 시 한국거래소 예비 심사와 금감원 증권신고서 심사 등 2단계를 거치는데, 단일종목 레버리지는 거래소 예비 심사가 끝나기도 전에 금감원이 심사했다고 지적했다. 이 영향으로 ETF 상장 심사가 평균 62일, 대표 지수형

articles.title: 서울-수원공소청장 “李 공소취소 검토-협의한 적 없어”
articles.snippet: 검찰청이 폐지되면서 출범한 공소청에 대한 첫 국정감사에서는 이재명 대통령 관련 사건의 공소취소 가능성이 쟁점이 됐다. 이 대통령 사건의 공소유지를 맡은 서울중앙·수원지방공소청은 공소취소를 검토하거나 법무부와 협의한 적 없다고 밝혔다. 19일 국회 법제사법위원회 국정감사에서 박철우 서울중앙지방공소청장은 이 대통령 사건에 대한 공소취소 가능성을 묻는 질의에 “국민적 관심이 매우 높다는 건 알지만 여느 사건과 다를 바 없다”며 “개별 사건에 대해 어떻게 하겠다고 말씀드릴 수 없는 게 원칙”이라고 말했다. 김봉현 수원지방공소청장도 쌍방울 대북송금 사건을 두고 ‘(법무부 검찰인권존중미래위원회) 진상조사단에서 공소취소를 요청하면 응하겠느냐’는 질의에 “요청받은 적 없다”며 “사건이 재판 중에 있다”고 했다. 서울중앙지방공소청은 이 대통령의 대장동·백현동·위례신도시 개발 특혜 의혹 사건을, 수원지방공소청은 쌍방울 대북송금 의혹 사건과 경기도 법인카드 유용 사건 등의 공소유지를 맡고 있다. 다

articles.snippet: 도널드 트럼프 미국 대통령이 19일(현지 시간) 중국 선전에서 11월 열리는 아시아태평양경제협력체(APEC) 정상회의 참석을 계기로 김정은 북한 국무위원장과 만날 가능성에 대해 “모르겠다”고 밝혔다.트럼프 대통령은 이날 백악관에서 기자들과 만난 자리에서 ‘다음 달 중국에서 북한 지도자와 만날 수 있다고 생각하나’라는 질의에 “나도 모르겠다”고 답했다. 그러면서 “누가 회담을 요청하고 있는지도 확실하지 않다(I’m not sure that anybody’s asking for a meeting)”고 덧붙였다.다만 그는 “나는 김정은 위원장과 아주 잘 지내고 있다(but my relationship with Kim Jong Un is very good)”며 김 위원장과의 친분이 여전히 두텁다고 주장했다. 트럼프 대통령의 이날 발언에 대해 불과 1주일 전과는 미묘한 온도차를 보이고 있는 평가가 나온다. 그는 12일(현지 시간) 백악관에서 ‘다음 달 아시아 방문 중 김 위원장과 만날

articles.title: 中 돌아가는 쌍둥이 판다, 12월 11일 마지막 공개
articles.snippet: 12월 중국으로 돌아가야 하는 에버랜드 쌍둥이 판다(사진) 루이바오와 후이바오를 국내에서 만날 수 있는 마지막 날이 잠정적으로 12월 11일로 정해졌다. 삼성물산 리조트 부문 에버랜드는 루이바오와 후이바오의 국제 이동을 위한 야생동물 사전 검역을 11월 13일 시작한다고 19일 밝혔다. 에버랜드 측은 “검역 절차에 들어가더라도 쌍둥이 판다는 관람객과 제한적 만남을 가질 수 있을 예정”이라며 “판다 세컨드 하우스는 외부와 완전히 차단된 실내 방사 시설이기 때문”이라고 설명했다. 다만 마지막 공개일을 포함한 관람 일정은 달라질 수 있다. 에버랜드는 두 판다의 건강 상태와 검역 진행 상황, 이송 준비 등을 살펴 공개 시간과 관람 방식을 조정할 방침이다. 쌍둥이 판다의 최종적인 중국 이송 날짜와 이동 장소 역시 기온과 현지 여건을 검토한 뒤 확정될 예정이다. 이들 판다는 2023년 7월 엄마 아이바오와 아빠 러바오 사이에서 태어난 국내 첫 쌍둥이 판다 자매로 화제를 낳았다.

articles.title: 바다 보며 맨발로 2.6km… 보령 해변서 힐링 걷기
articles.snippet: 충남 보령시는 최근 대천해수욕장 머드광장에서 시민과 관광객 600여 명이 참여한 가운데 ‘2026 해양치유 프로그램 개막식, 웰니스 해변 걷기 데이’를 열었다고 19일 밝혔다. 이번 행사는 보령의 바다와 해변 등 해양자원을 활용한 치유 프로그램을 알리고, 시민들의 건강한 걷기 실천과 해양치유 문화 확산을 도모하기 위해 마련됐다. 참가자들은 머드광장에서 노을광장까지 왕복 2.6km 해변을 맨발로 걸으며 보령의 자연 속에서 휴식과 활력을 느끼는 시간을 가졌다. 특히 보령시보건소에서 양성한 걷기 지도자와 걷기동아리 회원 26개 팀, 180여 명이 참여해 생활 속 걷기 문화 확산에 힘을 보탰다. 시민들은 일상에서 걷기를 실천하는 계기가 됐다. 행사장에서는 청년센터 체험부스, 건강홍보관 등 다양한 체험·홍보 프로그램도 함께 운영돼 참가자들의 호응을 얻었다. 또 모바일 걷기 애플리케이션(앱) ‘걷쥬’ 챌린지를 통해 미션을 달성한 참가자에게 모바일 쿠폰을 지급해 걷기의 재미와 성취감을 더했다.

articles.title: California to receive $6m settlement after 23andMe data breach
articles.snippet: Millions of customers’ genetic and personal information exposed in 2023, including more than 855,000 Californians California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, on Monday announced the state will receive a $6m settlement payment in 23andMe’s bankruptcy, resolving California’s legal claims related to a 2023 data breach that exposed 6.9 million customers’ ⁠genetic and other ⁠personal information. California had ​unsuccessfully tried to block the $305m sale of 23andMe assets to TTAM Research Institute, a non-profit controlled by the 23andMe ⁠co-founder Anne Wojcicki. The state had argued that the bankruptcy sale violated California’s Genetic Information Privacy Act, and it had said ⁠consumers did not give express consent to the sale. Continue reading...

articles.title: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan
articles.snippet: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday. Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”. Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”. The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status. Continue reading...

articles.title: JB Pritzker thinks AI could help us live to 100 — or threaten us like nukes
articles.snippet: Today, I’m talking with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has a lot of thoughts about AI, tech, and privacy. If you’ve been listening to the show, you know that one of my running theories is that those issues are driving a big and maybe kind of unexpected political realignment — and with the midterms coming up next month, and early voting already underway in a lot of places, the stakes are pretty high right now. So I asked Gov. Pritzker about all that, and he was surprisingly willing to dive right into the absolute existential weeds of what government is even for. You’ll hear him say — and it’s hard to disagree — that some problems are just collective action problems that require the government to do a lot of work. We can’t solve all these problems one at a time, or even one state at a time. It’s a pretty deep conversation, and we really got into it on a lot of issues. And of course, I had to ask him: Are the Bears gonna stay in Illinois? Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Here we go. Gov. JB Pritzker, you’re the governor of Illinois. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks, Nilay. Great to be with you. I am very excited to talk to you. We’re in the heart of midterm season. You are running for reelection. I have to tell you. I have to be very honest with you. I personally feel a lot of pressure in this interview, not only because I’m speaking to a governor, but because I went to school in Chicago. My sister still lives in Chicago. My wife grew up in Illinois. Her entire family is farmers in North Central Illinois. Boy, do I have a list of questions for you. I have to do a good job here. Well, we’re claiming you. Now that I know all that, we’re claiming you. You’re an Illinoisan. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. I don’t know about that. I grew up in Wisconsin. Here’s my first question for you. I’m a die-hard Packers fan. Are you going to let the Bears move to Indiana? That is not our intention. We are, in fact, in discussions with the Bears and the NFL about keeping the Bears either in Chicago or in Arlington Heights, but in Illinois. I’m saying, as a Packers fan, nothing is funnier than the outcome of the Bears moving to Indiana. I just want to put that out there. Openly biased in this case — I own two shares of that stock — but I’m going to make the comparison here. And the reason I started there is not only because I think that’s a funny outcome, although I do, but it feels like we are in the middle of a generational political realignment. I’m sure you feel that, in this election campaign, the idea of big business and how that should interact with the government, and how the government should be able to push back on big business and not give in to big business. All of that feels up for grabs. And the comparison I will make in this specific case is your fellow governor, Gavin Newsom, in California. They sued the Ellison family, Paramount, over the Warner Brothers merger. Paramount threatened to leave. They made a lot of noise about Nashville, Texas, Miami, or wherever you make noise about these days, and it feels like Newsom caved. It feels like he pressured his Attorney General, Rob Bonta, to settle that lawsuit and keep them there. They settled the lawsuit. The next day, the Ellison family is like, “We never… We’re from California. We would never leave.” I see a parallel here with the Bears that is connected to that larger realignment, how government and business should interact. Do you see that parallel? Do you feel that realignment? Well, what I can tell you is we’re pretty tough negotiators in Chicago and Illinois, and that’s really what we’re in the midst of now with the Bears. But I understand your point about realignment. I mean, there is a generational change, and I think it’s also an attitudinal change about protecting taxpayers, protecting people who frankly are among the most vulnerable to all the technology that’s overtaking people’s lives and invading people’s homes. And so I do believe that the government has to be more active now and become a fighter for our people and not just a collaborator with business on everything. I’m a businessman, as you know, before I became governor. But I also know that, for the people of Illinois anyway, my job is to protect the working people of this state who often don’t have anybody protecting them except a government that will stand up for them. So that’s kind of the realignment that I see. And that generational shift, I agree with you. It’s partly a Democratic Party generational shift. Generationally, we’re a little more aggressive. And I’m probably older than the next generation that’s already possibly taking office this November. I’m 61 years old, but I think of myself as having come out of the tech world and as somebody who has been a fighter for progressive values that, yeah, we’ve got to become more aggressive and make sure we’re standing up for our people. There are two places where I see the realignment in particular. One is data centers, one is privacy, and you just see that as a bipartisan backlash to those things. I would actually add a third, which is antitrust broadly. It’s weird if you go into Silicon Valley. David Sacks is retweeting Lina Khan from the Biden administration talking about whether the AI industry needs an antitrust exemption to manage safety. They both agree that these companies don’t need antitrust exemptions. They actually should be more competitive. Again, putting that in the context of regulating these companies, thinking about the dynamic between the government and the biggest companies in the world. I’ll just ask the question, I guess, more directly. Do you think Newsom was right to give in to Paramount, or do you think he should have forced them to make good on that threat to leave? I can’t speak to the Paramount situation well enough to give you an answer, so it would be unfair for me to do so. I can say once again that our orientation today — and I think about the big AI companies and the big social media companies as well — has to be like, wait a minute, too much power in too few hands. Particularly when we talk about AI, where it’s potentially existential, but certainly transformative, which is probably a kind way to say it about the economy, that we’re going to have to get very engaged. Guardrails, of course, on both parts, but also addressing what I think on the AI front is potentially a significant change in employment in the United States. I’m not somebody who is necessarily convinced that we have to see a whole bunch of job loss, but that does feel like that’s the direction this is going. What I’m suggesting is we better be prepared, and we better be protecting people who are going to lose their jobs, or at least it appears they’re going to lose their jobs. And I’ll just give you this thought. If these days 4 percent unemployment is kind of the acceptable near full employment number, I think the problem we’re going to see is — if that’s sort of the level that we’re going to hopefully aim for and stay at — that in very short order, we could end up at 7 percent and have that be the baseline, or maybe 10 percent. And if you think about what’s happened, the upheavals of economies and of governments when you get to 10 percent unemployment in any country. We better be focused on how we’re going to give people the dignity of work and enough income so that they can make a life for themselves when you’re going to put people out of work by virtue of this technology. By the way, much of the benefit of that is going to go to a very, very few people. So we’ve got to wrestle with that and come to a conclusion. I wanted to start with some of the brinksmanship we have seen in the negotiations between, particularly, states and the big companies, because that brinksmanship is real. The threat is we will leave. We just covered, I don’t know, Kevin O’Leary in Utah talking about data centers, and the people of Utah really pushed back against Kevin O’Leary building that data center. But his argument was, “Well, I’m just going to shop around.” This is what states do. They compete with tax incentives and benefits, maybe for data centers, which will put everyone out of a job. They compete for land use rights. You’ve got a rural state with a lot of farms in it. How are you thinking about that dynamic? Do you feel like you’re in competition with the other states, or is this bipartisan realignment creating more of a level playing field where these companies are going to have to actually give something? We are in competition. We just are because it isn’t bipartisan, at least if you ask me. Unless there is a change in the government.
